profiles.name: Karl Swenson
profiles.excerpt: Karl Swenson built his career in radio before film and television made his face familiar, moving from daytime serials and mystery drama to Broadway and later character roles.
profiles.bio_html:
Karl Swenson was born in Brooklyn in 1908 to Swedish parents. He initially studied for a medical career at Marietta College but left that path for acting, building stage experience in New York and becoming a regular radio performer during the 1930s and 1940s.

Radio gave Swenson broad professional range, from daytime serials such as Lorenzo Jones and Portia Faces Life to mystery and anthology programs including Inner Sanctum Mysteries, Columbia Workshop and The Mercury Theatre on the Air. He also played the title role in a 1945 radio version of Father Brown. His later screen career included westerns, the voice of Merlin in Disney's The Sword in the Stone, and Lars Hanson on Little House on the Prairie.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 13 Inner Sanctum Mysteries performances credited to Swenson, seven Suspense appearances, six Columbia Workshop broadcasts, four Words at War episodes and additional work on CBS Radio Mystery Theater, Luke Slaughter of Tombstone, Molle Mystery Theatre and The Chase.

profiles.name: Ken Lynch
profiles.excerpt: Ken Lynch was a radio actor before television made him a familiar authority figure, with recurring roles that stretched from adventure serials to crime drama and westerns.
profiles.bio_html:
Ken Lynch was born in Cleveland in 1910 and built his acting career first on radio. His early work included the Gargoyle, an ex-convict who assisted the title clergyman on The Bishop and the Gargoyle, and Tank Tanker on the aviation adventure serial Hop Harrigan.

Lynch also worked in daytime serials and later became a dependable crime and western actor. Radio credits included The Falcon, 21st Precinct, Gunsmoke and Cafe Istanbul. Television later used the same stern, practical presence for policemen, detectives and other authority figures, but that screen type grew from years of microphone work.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 17 The Falcon performances credited to Lynch, six The Chase appearances, five Gunsmoke episodes, four each on Gang Busters and Have Gun, Will Travel, three each on Inner Sanctum Mysteries and Words at War, plus two Molle Mystery Theatre appearances.

profiles.name: Nestor Paiva
profiles.excerpt: Nestor Paiva combined stage and radio experience with one of Hollywood's busiest supporting-screen careers, bringing a powerful character voice to drama, westerns and adventure.
profiles.bio_html:
Nestor Paiva was born in Fresno, California in 1905 to Portuguese immigrant parents and studied at the University of California, Berkeley, where he performed in stage productions. Radio and theatre became early professional outlets before film work expanded his career.

Paiva eventually appeared in hundreds of motion pictures and television episodes, often as officials, sea captains, bartenders and other strongly drawn supporting characters. Radio used the same vocal authority on literary adaptations, westerns and suspense programs. His later screen roles included Captain Lucas in Creature from the Black Lagoon and Teo Gonzales in Disney's Zorro.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten NBC University Theater performances credited to Paiva, seven Roy Rogers appearances, four each on Night Beat and Wild Bill Hickok, and three each on Escape, Fibber McGee and Molly, Gunsmoke and Tales of the Texas Rangers.

profiles.name: Tim Graham
profiles.excerpt: Tim Graham was a working Hollywood character actor whose radio credits span prestige anthology, detective drama and several major western series.
profiles.bio_html:
Tim Graham was born in Kansas in 1904 and built a long supporting career in film, television and radio. He rarely occupied star billing, but his work placed him inside the professional character-actor pool that Hollywood studios and network radio drew on constantly.

Radio used Graham across very different formats, from feature-film adaptations on Lux Radio Theatre to detective stories and westerns. His surviving credits show repeated work on Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, Have Gun, Will Travel, Roy Rogers and Wild Bill Hickok, reflecting a performer valued for reliability and range rather than one signature role.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves eight Lux Radio Theatre performances credited to Graham, seven Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances, six each on Have Gun, Will Travel, Roy Rogers and Wild Bill Hickok, three each on Fort Laramie and Let George Do It, plus additional Tales of the Texas Rangers work.

profiles.name: Donn Reed
profiles.excerpt: Donn Reed turned reporting into radio drama on Nightwatch, originating and producing a series built from real police calls before continuing a long broadcast-news career.
profiles.bio_html:
Donn Reed was a Los Angeles broadcaster whose career joined acting, reporting and production. After serving as a B-17 navigator during World War II, he returned to radio and developed the concept that became Nightwatch, riding with Culver City police and recording real incidents rather than relying on conventional studio scripts.

Reed originated the program, produced it and served as its on-air reporter, making Nightwatch a distinctive hybrid of documentary, journalism and dramatic radio. He later worked in airborne traffic reporting and nightly news for KABC, then taught broadcast journalism after retirement. His announcing and production work are therefore substantial professional branches, not incidental credits.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 45 Nightwatch broadcasts credited to Reed. That concentrated collection documents one of radio's most striking experiments in turning actual police work into immediate, location-recorded broadcasting.

profiles.name: Nat Polen
profiles.excerpt: Nat Polen bridged classic network radio and its 1970s revival, building a durable acting career that also made him a familiar daytime television doctor.
profiles.bio_html:
Nat Polen was born in Brooklyn in 1914 and developed a career across radio, stage and television. By the 1950s he was working in New York broadcasting, where experienced actors moved regularly between live dramatic radio and the rapidly expanding television industry.

Polen became widely known on television for long-running medical roles on As the World Turns and One Life to Live, but radio remained part of his professional life. He appeared in science fiction and anthology drama and later became a recurring member of the CBS Radio Mystery Theater company during the 1970s revival of network radio drama.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 33 CBS Radio Mystery Theater performances credited to Polen, six Theater Five appearances, two each on X Minus One and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, and additional work on 2000 Plus and The Mysterious Traveler.

profiles.name: Tudor Owen
profiles.excerpt: Tudor Owen was a Welsh character actor whose Jocko Madigan on Pat Novak for Hire became one of Jack Webb's most memorable radio partnerships.
profiles.bio_html:
Tudor Owen was born in Wales in 1898 and worked in film and theatre before becoming a prolific radio character actor in the 1940s and 1950s. His heavy, expressive voice made him especially effective as seamen, policemen, doctors and other rough-edged supporting figures.

His defining radio role was Jocko Madigan, the alcoholic former doctor and philosophical waterfront companion to Jack Webb's title detective on Pat Novak, for Hire. Owen also worked with Webb on Johnny Modero, Pier 23 and Pete Kelly's Blues, while appearing broadly across anthology and detective radio. Later audiences heard him as Towser in Disney's One Hundred and One Dalmatians.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves ten Pat Novak, for Hire performances credited to Owen, nine Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar appearances, six each on Escape, NBC University Theater and Night Beat, four Lux Radio Theatre broadcasts and three Crime Classics episodes.

profiles.name: Wendell Holmes
profiles.excerpt: Wendell Holmes was a high-volume New York radio professional whose career ranged from Dr. Watson to some of X Minus One's most celebrated science-fiction broadcasts.
profiles.bio_html:
Wendell Holmes was born in Ohio in 1914, graduated from Ohio State University at a young age and went to New York rather than entering education. He began professional radio work in 1934 and later recalled the extraordinary pace of the business, describing an early period when he was appearing on dozens of broadcasts.

Holmes worked in serials, mysteries and anthology drama and played Dr. Watson opposite John Stanley in the late-1940s radio Sherlock Holmes, using the pseudonym George Spelvin to avoid confusion with the fictional detective's surname. Science fiction became another major branch of his career. He appeared repeatedly on Dimension X and especially X Minus One, including adaptations of Ray Bradbury and other leading genre writers.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 26 X Minus One performances credited to Holmes, four each on Dimension X and The Mysterious Traveler, three The Chase appearances, two each on Gang Busters and Stroke of Fate, and additional work on CBS Radio Workshop and Molle Mystery Theatre.

profiles.name: Mary Shipp
profiles.excerpt: Mary Shipp was a versatile radio actress who moved from juvenile roles into comedy, detective drama and television, with Miss Spalding on The Great Gildersleeve among her best-known parts.
profiles.bio_html:
Mary Shipp was born in Los Angeles in 1915, studied ballet as a child and entered stock theatre at an early age. She later studied dramatics at Los Angeles City College, and radio became the central medium of her early professional career.

Shipp first worked in radio as Becky Thatcher in The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and later played Kathleen on The Aldrich Family, appeared opposite Milton Berle, and became Miss Spalding on The Great Gildersleeve. Her range extended well beyond comedy, with detective and suspense performances across the West Coast repertory. She also wrote occasionally, including scripts sold to Kate Smith Speaks, though acting remained her principal profession.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 22 The Great Gildersleeve performances credited to Shipp, four Broadway Is My Beat appearances, three each on Escape, The Adventures of Philip Marlowe and Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, two each on Richard Diamond, Private Detective and Screen Directors Playhouse, plus additional anthology work.

profiles.name: Paul Richards
profiles.excerpt: Paul Richards brought formal theatre training to radio crime drama before becoming a prolific television character actor known for intense and often dangerous roles.
profiles.bio_html:
Paul Richards was born Paul Richard Levitt in Hollywood in 1924 and studied theatre at UCLA, eventually earning a graduate degree in the field. Radio became one of the early professional arenas in which he developed the controlled intensity that later defined many of his screen roles.

Richards worked repeatedly in West Coast crime and detective drama, including Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar, This Is Your FBI, Dragnet and The Six Shooter. Television later made him a familiar guest actor in westerns, crime shows and science fiction, but his radio work shows the same ability to establish tension and character quickly through voice alone.

Golden Radio Hour currently preserves 20 Yours Truly, Johnny Dollar performances credited to Richards, eight This Is Your FBI appearances, three each on Dragnet and The Six Shooter, two each on A Man Called X, Barrie Craig and Escape, plus additional work on Broadway Is My Beat.
